neutral_facts.value: The accused, a partnership firm, obtained contracts for data entry work and subcontracted the work to the complainant. The complainant was paid a caution deposit and completed the data entry work. The accused issued cheques for the payment, which were dishonoured due to insufficient funds. The accused assured the complainant that the cheques would be honoured on re-presentation. The complainant presented the cheques again, but they were returned unpaid. The complainant issued a notice of demand for payment, which was not fulfilled. The complainant filed a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The High Court quashed the complaint, but the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, finding that the complaint contained sufficient averments to meet the requirements of Section 141.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the complaint contained sufficient averments to meet the requirements of Section 141(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, and that the High Court was in error in quashing the complaint against the first respondent.

quotes.text: The complaint contains a recital of the fact that the first set of cheques were returned for insufficiency of funds. The complaint also contains an averment that after the second set of cheques were dishonoured, the accused assured the complainant that they will be honoured on re-presentation in the month of July 2011. The averments are sufficient to meet the requirement of Section 141(1).

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the High Court was correct in quashing the complaint as there was no averment that the first respondent was in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of the business, and that the first respondent had no day-to-day connection with the partnership firm.

quotes.text: The submission is that there was no averment in the complaint that the first respondent was in charge of and was responsible to the 'company' for the conduct of the business.

In these circumstances, learned counsel submitted that the High Court having quashed the complaint, this Court ought not to exercise its jurisdiction under Article 136 to interfere with the judgment and order of the High Court.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that a partnership firm is included within the definition of 'company' under Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and that the complaint must be read holistically to determine if it meets the requirements of Section 141(1).

quotes.text: In terms of the explanation to s.141, the expression 'company' is defined to mean any body corporate and include a firm or other association of individuals.
The issue is whether there are sufficient averments in the complaint to meet the requirement of Section 141(1). This is a matter which has to be determined on a holistic reading of the complaint.
